content:
# Deployment and Self-Hosting (Docker and Cloud Basics) ##### "It works on my machine" A student built a superb n8n workflow on their laptop — order processing, AI classification, database writes, the lot. They demoed it to a client, who loved it and asked one question: *"So it runs even when your laptop is closed, right?"* It did not. It ran on `localhost:5678`, on a machine that goes to sleep during lectures and moves to a different Wi-Fi network twice a day. The gap between "I built an automation" and "an automation is running" is **deployment** — putting your work somewhere that stays up, survives restarts, keeps its data, and can be reached from the internet. This is the skill that separates a student project from a service, and it is genuinely worth learning even if you mostly use managed platforms: understanding what a hosted product does for you is how you decide whether you need it. ##### Managed cloud versus self-hosted Both are legitimate. The question is which trade-offs you want. **Managed** (Zapier, Make, n8n Cloud): you pay a subscription and someone else handles servers, uptime, upgrades, backups, scaling and security patches. You get started in minutes and never think about infrastructure. **Self-hosted**: you run the software on a machine you control. You pay for a server (₹400–1,500/month for a small VPS handles a surprising amount) instead of per execution, your data never leaves your infrastructure, and you can customize freely — install npm packages, mount local files, connect to internal networks. In exchange, uptime, backups, upgrades and security are your job. The honest calculation: self-hosting is cheaper in *money* and more expensive in *time*. A ₹500/month VPS replacing a ₹8,000/month plan looks like an obvious win until you spend a Saturday recovering from a failed upgrade you had no backup for. Choose self-hosting when you have a real reason — data residency, high volume, custom code, internal network access — not merely because it is cheaper. ##### Docker basics Docker is the technology that makes self-hosting reasonable, and the mental model is worth getting right. **Image** — a read-only template containing an application and everything it needs: code, runtime, libraries, configuration. Think of it as a recipe, or a class in programming terms. `docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n` is an image. **Container** — a running instance of an image. Think of it as the cooked dish, or an object instantiated from a class. You can run several containers from one image, and each is isolated from the others and from the host. **Volume** — persistent storage attached to a container. This matters enormously: **containers are ephemeral**. Delete a container and everything inside it disappears. A volume lives outside the container's lifecycle, so your workflows and credentials survive restarts and upgrades. **Compose** — a tool that describes a multi-container setup in one YAML file so you can start everything with a single command, rather than typing long `docker run` lines and remembering them. Why containers rather than virtual machines? A VM virtualizes an entire operating system; a container shares the host kernel and isolates only the application. The result is dramatically lighter — containers start in seconds and use a fraction of the memory. Performance studies (Felter et al., 2015) found container overhead to be near-negligible compared with running natively, which is why the industry moved this way. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Dockerfile / registry] -->|build or pull| B[Image
read-only template] B -->|docker run| C[Container 1
n8n] B -->|docker run| D[Container 2
n8n staging] C --- V[(Volume
persistent data)] E[docker-compose.yml] -->|defines & starts| C E -->|defines & starts| F[Container
PostgreSQL] F --- W[(Volume
db data)] ``` ##### Self-hosting n8n with Docker Compose Here is a production-shaped setup — n8n backed by PostgreSQL rather than the default SQLite, which matters once you have real execution volume. ```yaml # docker-compose.yml services: postgres: image: postgres:16-alpine restart: unless-stopped environment: POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER} POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} POSTGRES_DB: n8n volumes: - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d n8n"] interval: 10s timeout: 5s retries: 5 n8n: image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:latest restart: unless-stopped depends_on: postgres: condition: service_healthy ports: - "5678:5678" environment: # --- database --- DB_TYPE: postgresdb DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST: postgres DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE: n8n DB_POSTGRESDB_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER} DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} # --- security --- N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY: ${N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY} N8N_BASIC_AUTH_ACTIVE: "true" N8N_BASIC_AUTH_USER: ${N8N_USER} N8N_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD: ${N8N_PASSWORD} # --- URLs and timezone --- N8N_HOST: ${N8N_HOST} N8N_PROTOCOL: https WEBHOOK_URL: https://${N8N_HOST}/ GENERIC_TIMEZONE: Asia/Kolkata TZ: Asia/Kolkata # --- housekeeping --- EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE: "true" EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE: "336" # hours (14 days) volumes: - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n - ./local-files:/files volumes: postgres_data: n8n_data: ``` With a `.env` file beside it (gitignored, naturally): ```bash POSTGRES_USER=n8n POSTGRES_PASSWORD=a-long-random-password N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=another-long-random-string-keep-this-safe N8N_USER=admin N8N_PASSWORD=a-strong-admin-password N8N_HOST=automation.yourdomain.com ``` Then: ```bash docker compose up -d # start everything in the background docker compose ps # what's running docker compose logs -f n8n # follow the logs docker compose pull && docker compose up -d # upgrade to a newer image docker compose down # stop (volumes and data survive) docker compose down -v # stop AND DELETE volumes — destroys your data ``` Three details in that file deserve emphasis. **`N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY`** encrypts your stored credentials — lose it and every saved credential becomes unreadable, so back it up separately from the data. **`restart: unless-stopped`** makes containers come back automatically after a crash or a server reboot. And **execution pruning** stops your database growing without limit, which is the most common cause of a self-hosted instance slowly dying. ##### Deploying to the cloud Two routes, depending on how much you want to manage. **A cloud VM** (DigitalOcean Droplet, AWS EC2, Hetzner, Linode) gives you full control. The outline: ```bash ssh root@your-server-ip # 1. install Docker curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh # 2. create a non-root user and lock down SSH keys (do this properly) adduser deploy && usermod -aG docker deploy # 3. copy your compose file and .env, then start docker compose up -d # 4. firewall: allow only what you need ufw allow OpenSSH && ufw allow 80 && ufw allow 443 && ufw enable ``` You then need **HTTPS**, which is non-negotiable for anything handling webhooks or credentials. The easy path is a reverse proxy — Caddy is the simplest (it obtains and renews Let's Encrypt certificates automatically with a two-line config), with Nginx Proxy Manager and Traefik as popular alternatives. Point a domain's DNS at the server's IP, and the proxy handles the rest. **A platform-as-a-service** (Railway, Render, Fly.io) skips most of that: connect a repository or pick a template, set environment variables in a web UI, and it builds, deploys, provides HTTPS and a domain, and restarts on failure. You pay more than a raw VPS and give up some control, but for a first deployment it removes an enormous amount of yak-shaving. This is what I would recommend for your first real deployment. ##### Environment variables, backups, and uptime **Environment variables** are how you configure a container without changing the image. The same image runs in dev and prod with different databases, credentials and URLs. Keep them in a gitignored `.env` for Compose, or in the platform's secret manager for PaaS. **Backups** are the part beginners skip and regret. A self-hosted instance with no backup is a countdown timer. You need three things backed up: 1. The **database** (workflow definitions, credentials, execution history). 2. The **`.n8n` volume**. 3. The **encryption key** — stored somewhere *other* than the server. ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # backup.sh — run nightly via cron set -euo pipefail STAMP=$(date +%F) BACKUP_DIR=/opt/backups mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR" # database dump docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" n8n \ | gzip > "$BACKUP_DIR/n8n-db-$STAMP.sql.gz" # volume archive docker run --rm -v n8n_data:/data -v "$BACKUP_DIR":/backup alpine \ tar czf "/backup/n8n-files-$STAMP.tar.gz" -C /data . # ship offsite and prune local copies older than 14 days rclone copy "$BACKUP_DIR" remote:n8n-backups find "$BACKUP_DIR" -type f -mtime +14 -delete ``` Add it to cron with `0 2 * * * /opt/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1`. And then — the step everyone skips — **restore from a backup once** to prove it works. An untested backup is a hypothesis. **Uptime** comes from four things: `restart: unless-stopped` policies, health checks, an external uptime monitor (UptimeRobot or Healthchecks.io pinging your instance every five minutes and alerting when it stops responding), and resource headroom — 2 GB RAM minimum for n8n plus Postgres, more if you run browser automation. ##### Common pitfalls - **No volume** — workflows vanish on restart. The single most common Docker mistake. - **`docker compose down -v`** in production. That `-v` deletes your data. - **Losing the encryption key** — credentials become permanently unreadable. - **Exposing port 5678 to the internet with no auth or HTTPS** — your credential store is behind that URL. - **No backups, or untested backups.** - **`latest` image tag** in production — an unattended pull can bring a breaking change. Pin a version. - **No execution pruning** — the database grows until the disk fills. - **Undersized servers** — n8n on 512 MB RAM will be killed by the OOM reaper under load. - **Secrets committed** in `docker-compose.yml` instead of `.env`. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: install Docker, then use a **docker-compose file to run n8n locally with persistent storage**, configure it with **environment variables**, and confirm a workflow **survives a restart**. Test that last part deliberately: build a workflow, run `docker compose down`, then `docker compose up -d`, and check it is still there. If it is gone, your volume is misconfigured — and finding that out on your laptop is much better than finding out in production. The mini project is the real deployment: put a self-hosted n8n on a **cloud VM or a platform like Railway/Render**, secure it with environment variables, set up a **backup**, add a **restart policy**, and run one real workflow **end to end**. Getting a webhook to hit your own server over HTTPS from the public internet is a genuine milestone — it means you have built infrastructure, not just a workflow. For the assignment, explain **images, containers and Compose** in plain terms (template / running instance / multi-container orchestrator, with the recipe-and-dish analogy) and write your **self-hosted vs n8n Cloud comparison** covering cost, control and maintenance. Be honest about the maintenance column; a recommendation that acknowledges the Saturday-afternoon upgrade risk is far more credible than one that pretends self-hosting is free. ##### Key takeaways - Deployment is what turns a workflow on your laptop into a service that runs whether you are awake or not. - An image is a template, a container is a running instance, a volume is the persistent storage that lets data survive both — and Compose defines the whole stack in one file. - Self-host for data residency, volume economics, custom code and internal access; use managed platforms when you would rather not own uptime. - Configure everything through environment variables, back up the database, the volume and the encryption key separately, and test a restore. - Never expose a self-hosted instance without HTTPS and authentication, pin your image versions, prune execution history, and monitor uptime externally.
